questions.question: What are the rules for `this` binding in JavaScript?
questions.title: This Binding Rules
questions.direct_answer: Five rules, in precedence order: (1) new — this is the new object; (2) explicit — call/apply/bind's first argument (bind wins durably); (3) implicit — the receiver: obj.method() binds this=obj; (4) default — undefined in strict mode, globalThis in sloppy; (5) arrows have NO this — they capture the enclosing scope's this at write time, forever. The gotchas: method extracted from object loses its receiver (this becomes default); passing obj.method as a callback detaches it.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q{how was it called?}
    Q -->|new| N[this = new instance]
    Q -->|call apply bind| E[this = given ctx — bind locks forever]
    Q -->|obj.method| I[this = obj — receiver]
    Q -->|plain call| D[this = undefined strict / globalThis sloppy]
    Q -->|arrow function| A[NO this — captured from write-time scope]
    DET[obj.method passed as callback] -.detached.-> D
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why this exists as a mechanism (the design rationale): this enables method reuse across receivers — one getName function works for any object shaped {name}. The alternative (explicit receiver parameter, like Python's self) makes every method signature carry it; JS chose implicit binding + the prototype chain's shared methods to pair with it. The cost: binding depends on the CALL SITE's shape, so extracting/detaching changes behavior invisibly — the entire class of this-bugs.

The class-fields resolution (the modern corner): class methods are PROTOTYPE methods (this = instance when called as method), but class FIELDS with arrow functions (field = () => {...}) are per-INSTANCE arrows capturing construction-time this — pre-bound, detach-proof, at the memory cost of a function per instance (1000 instances = 1000 arrow functions vs 1 prototype method). The trade-off shows up in 'why does my team ban arrow class fields for methods but allow them for handlers?'

The historical arc worth one sentence (the close): JS moved from this-everywhere (prototype + class components) to this-free (function components + hooks close over props/state as ordinary variables, closures replace binding). The interview-level summary: know the five rules because legacy code and libraries still live on them; write new code where binding never comes up (arrows + closures), and detach bugs become impossible by construction.

questions.title: This Keyword Javascript

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OBJ[obj.method()] →|dot syntax| O[this = obj]
    FN[fn()] →|plain call| U[this = undefined or global]
    AR[arrow fn] →|lexical| I[inherits creation-scope this]
    CALL[fn.call obj] →|explicit| E[this = obj]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The binding semantics' reason for the confusion (the historical context): JavaScript's this predates classes — the design was for shared methods on objects where the receiver provides the context. The rules follow from the CALL-SITE syntax (how you invoke determines what this is), which is unlike Java/C++ where this is the instance pointer bound at definition.

The arrow function's [[ThisMode]] (the spec detail for depth): arrows are created with lexical this — their [[Environment]] captures the this of the enclosing function at CREATION time. They don't just 'not have this' — they're lexically scoped TO it, exactly like closures capture outer variables. The call/apply/bind on an arrow does nothing to this (the spec defines arrows as non-bindable).

The class-method trap (the modern follow-up): class methods (not arrow fields) are PROTOTYPES — this is call-site-bound. A method extracted and passed as a callback (this.handleClick as a prop) loses this. The fixes: constructor binding, the class-fields arrow (handleClick = () => { ... } — a class field that's an arrow, bound to the instance at construction). The class-fields pattern is the React idiom.
